Main.sentence: Columbia University in the City of New York ,  commonly referred to as Columbia University , is a ___E:private U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_university)___ ___E:Ivy League U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivy_League)___ ___E:research university U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university)___ in ___E:New York City U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City)___ .

It was first established in 1754 as King's College by ___E:royal charter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_charter)___ under ___E:George II of Great Britain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_II_of_Great_Britain)___ on the grounds of ___E:Trinity Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_Church_(Manhattan))___ in ___E:Manhattan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan)___ .

The university was renamed ___E:Columbia College U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_College_(New_York))___ in 1784 following the ___E:American Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution)___ , and in 1787 was placed under ___E:a private board of trustees U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trustees_of_Columbia_University_in_the_City_of_New_York)___ headed by former students ___E:Alexander Hamilton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Hamilton)___ and ___E:John Jay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jay)___ .
In 1896, the campus was moved to its current location in ___E:Morningside Heights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morningside_Heights)___ and renamed Columbia University.

It is the oldest institution of higher education in ___E:New York U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state))___ and the fifth- ___E:oldest in the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_university_in_the_United_States)___ .
Columbia is organized into twenty schools, including three undergraduate schools and sixteen graduate schools.

The university's research efforts include the ___E:Lamont–Doherty Earth Observatory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamont%E2%80%93Doherty_Earth_Observatory)___ , the ___E:Goddard Institute for Space Studies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goddard_Institute_for_Space_Studies)___ , and accelerator laboratories with ___E:Big Tech U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Tech)___ firms such as ___E:Amazon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_(company))___ and ___E:IBM U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM)___ .

Columbia is a founding member of the ___E:Association of American Universities U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_American_Universities)___ and was the first school in the United States to grant the ___E:MD degree U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Medicine)___ .
The university also administers and annually awards the ___E:Pulitzer Prize U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize)___ .

Columbia scientists and scholars have played a pivotal role in scientific breakthroughs including ___E:brain–computer interface U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brain%E2%80%93computer_interface)___ ; the ___E:laser U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser)___ and ___E:maser U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maser)___ ;   ___E:nuclear magnetic resonance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_magnetic_resonance)___ ;  the first ___E:nuclear pile U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_reactor)___ ; the first ___E:nuclear fission U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fission)___ reaction in the ___E:Americas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americas)___ ; the first evidence for ___E:plate tectonics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plate_tectonics)___ and ___E:continental drift U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_drift)___ ;    and much of the initial research and planning for the ___E:Manhattan Project U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Project)___ during ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ .

As of December 2021 [update] , its alumni, faculty, and staff have included 7 of the ___E:Founding Fathers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_Fathers_of_the_United_States)___ of the United States of America; [a] ___E:4 U.S. presidents U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_education)___ ; [b] 34 foreign ___E:heads of state or government U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_state)___ ; [c] 2 secretaries-general of the United Nations; [n 1] 10 justices of the ___E:United States Supreme Court U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States)___ ; ___E:103 Nobel laureates U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_affiliated_with_Columbia_University_as_alumni_or_faculty)___ ; 125 ___E:National Academy of Sciences U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Academy_of_Sciences)___ members;  53 living billionaires;  ___E:23 Olympic medalists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_American_universities_with_Olympic_medals)___ ;  33 ___E:Academy Award U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards)___ winners; and 125 Pulitzer Prize recipients.
Discussions regarding the founding of a college in the ___E:Province of New York U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_New_York)___ began as early as 1704.

Classes were initially held in July 1754 and were presided over by the college's first president, ___E:Samuel Johnson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Johnson_(American_educator))___ who was an Anglican Priest.  : 8–10  : 3 The college was officially founded on October 31, 1754, as King's College by royal charter of ___E:George II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_II_of_Great_Britain)___ ,   making it the oldest institution of higher learning in the ___E:State of New York U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_New_York)___ and the fifth oldest in the United States.

In 1763, Johnson was succeeded in the presidency by ___E:Myles Cooper U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myles_Cooper)___ , a graduate of ___E:The Queen's College, Oxford U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Queen%27s_College,_Oxford)___ , and an ardent ___E:Tory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tories_(British_political_party))___ .

In the charged political climate of the ___E:American Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution)___ , his chief opponent in discussions at the college was an undergraduate of the class of 1777, ___E:Alexander Hamilton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Hamilton)___ .  : 3 The ___E:Irish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_people)___ anatomist, ___E:Samuel Clossy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Clossy)___ , was appointed professor of natural philosophy in October 1765 and later the college's first professor of anatomy in 1767.

The ___E:American Revolutionary War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War)___ broke out in 1776, and was catastrophic for the operation of King's College, which suspended instruction for eight years beginning in 1776 with the arrival of the ___E:Continental Army U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Army)___ .

The suspension continued through the military occupation of New York City by British troops until their ___E:departure U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evacuation_Day_(New_York))___ in 1783. The college's library was looted and its sole building requisitioned for use as a military hospital first by American and then British forces.
The legislature agreed to assist the college, and on May 1, 1784, it passed "an Act for granting certain privileges to the College heretofore called King's College".

The Act created ___E:a board of regents U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_Regents_of_the_University_of_the_State_of_New_York)___ to oversee the resuscitation of King's College, and, in an effort to demonstrate its support for the new Republic, the legislature stipulated that "the College within the City of New York heretofore called King's College be forever hereafter called and known by the name of ___E:Columbia College U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_College_of_Columbia_University)___ ",  a reference to ___E:Columbia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_(personification))___ , an alternative name for America which in turn comes from the name of ___E:Christopher Columbus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Columbus)___ .

The Regents finally became aware of the college's defective constitution in February 1787 and appointed a revision committee, which was headed by ___E:John Jay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jay)___ and Alexander Hamilton.

In April of that same year, a new charter was adopted for the college granted the power to ___E:a separate board of 24 trustees U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trustees_of_Columbia_University_in_the_City_of_New_York)___ .  : 65–70

For a period in the 1790s, with New York City as the federal and state capital and the country under successive ___E:Federalist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federalist_Party_(United_States))___ governments, a revived Columbia thrived under the auspices of Federalists such as Hamilton and Jay. President ___E:George Washington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington)___ and Vice President ___E:John Adams U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Adams)___ , in addition to both houses of ___E:Congress U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress)___ attended ___E:the college's commencement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_commencement)___ on May 6, 1789, as a tribute of honor to the many alumni of the school who had been involved in the ___E:American Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution)___ .  : 74

In November 1813, the college agreed to incorporate its medical school with The College of Physicians and Surgeons, a new school created by the Regents of New York, forming ___E:Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_College_of_Physicians_and_Surgeons)___ .  : 53–60 In 1857, the college moved from the King's College campus at Park Place to a primarily ___E:Gothic Revival U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_Revival)___ campus on 49th Street and ___E:Madison Avenue U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Avenue)___ , where it remained for the next forty years.

During the last half of the 19th century, under the presidency of ___E:Frederick A. P. Barnard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_A._P._Barnard)___ , for whom ___E:Barnard College U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnard_College)___ is named, the institution rapidly assumed the shape of a modern university.
Barnard College was created in 1889 as a response to the university's refusal to accept women.

In 1896, university president ___E:Seth Low U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seth_Low)___ moved the campus from 49th Street to its present location, a more spacious campus in the developing neighborhood of ___E:Morningside Heights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morningside_Heights)___ .

Under the leadership of Low's successor, ___E:Nicholas Murray Butler U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Murray_Butler)___ , who served for over four decades, Columbia rapidly became the nation's major institution for research, setting the multiversity model that later universities would adopt.

Prior to becoming the president of Columbia University, Butler founded ___E:Teachers College U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teachers_College)___ , as a school to prepare home economists and manual art teachers for the children of the poor, with philanthropist ___E:Grace Hoadley Dodge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_Hoadley_Dodge)___ .
Teachers College is currently affiliated as the university's Graduate School of Education.

On March 8, 1917, as a result of America's entrance into ___E:World War 1 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_1)___ , Columbia president Nicholas Murray Butler formed the Columbia Reserve Officers Training Corps.
All students over the age of 18 who passed a physical exam were entered into this program.
Within 4 months, over 1,400 students were enrolled within the program.
They were one of 12 universities designated by the War department to create a naval section for the Student Army Training Corps.
As part of this new program, the US Army charged Columbia to create a "War Issues" course.

In 1919, a similar course was created for Columbia students, a "peace issues" course that evolved into "Introduction to Contemporary Civilization in the West", part of the university's ___E:core curriculum for undergraduate students U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Core_Curriculum_(Columbia_College))___ .

In the 1940s, faculty members, including ___E:John R. Dunning U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_R._Dunning)___ , ___E:I. I. Rabi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isidor_Isaac_Rabi)___ , ___E:Enrico Fermi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrico_Fermi)___ , and ___E:Polykarp Kusch U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polykarp_Kusch)___ , began what became the ___E:Manhattan Project U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Project)___ , creating the first nuclear fission reactor in the ___E:Americas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americas)___ and researching ___E:gaseous diffusion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaseous_diffusion)___ .

In 1928, ___E:Seth Low Junior College U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seth_Low_Junior_College)___ was established by Columbia University in order to mitigate the number of Jewish applicants to Columbia College.

The college was closed in 1936 due to the adverse effects of the ___E:Great Depression U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression)___ and its students were subsequently taught at Morningside Heights, although they did not belong to any college but to the university at large.
There was an evening school called University Extension, which taught night classes, for a fee, to anyone willing to attend.

In 1947, the program was reorganized as an undergraduate college and designated the ___E:School of General Studies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_of_General_Studies)___ in response to the return of ___E:GIs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GI_(military))___ after ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ .

In 1995, the School of General Studies was again reorganized as a full-fledged liberal arts college for ___E:non-traditional students U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-traditional_students)___ (those who have had an academic break of one year or more, or are pursuing dual-degrees) and was fully integrated into Columbia's traditional undergraduate curriculum.

The same year, the Division of Special Programs, later called the School of Continuing Education and now the ___E:School of Professional Studies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_School_of_Professional_Studies)___ , was established to reprise the former role of University Extension.

While the School of Professional Studies only offered non-degree programs for lifelong learners and high school students in its earliest stages, it now offers degree programs in a diverse range of professional and inter-disciplinary fields.

In the aftermath of World War II, the discipline of international relations became a major scholarly focus of the university, and in response, the ___E:School of International and Public Affairs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_School_of_International_and_Public_Affairs)___ was founded in 1946, drawing upon the resources of the faculties of political science, economics, and history.
The ___E:Columbia University Bicentennial U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_Bicentennial)___ was celebrated in 1954.

During the 1960s, student activism reached a climax with ___E:protests in the spring of 1968 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_protests_of_1968)___ , when hundreds of students occupied buildings on campus.
The incident forced the resignation of Columbia's president, ___E:Grayson Kirk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grayson_Kirk)___ , and the establishment of the University Senate.

Though several schools in the university had admitted women for years, Columbia College first admitted women in the fall of 1983,  after a decade of failed negotiations with ___E:Barnard College U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnard_College)___ , the all-female institution affiliated with the university, to merge the two schools.

Barnard College still remains affiliated with Columbia, and all Barnard graduates are issued diplomas signed by the ___E:presidents of Columbia University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Columbia_University)___ and Barnard College.
During the late 20th century, the university underwent significant academic, structural, and administrative changes as it developed into a major research university.
For much of the 19th century, the university consisted of decentralized and separate faculties specializing in Political Science, Philosophy, and Pure Science.
In 1979, these faculties were merged into the ___E:Graduate School of Arts and Sciences U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Graduate_School_of_Arts_and_Sciences)___ .

In 1991, the faculties of Columbia College, the School of General Studies, the Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, the ___E:School of the Arts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_School_of_the_Arts)___ , and the ___E:School of Professional Studies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_School_of_Professional_Studies)___ were merged into the Faculty of Arts and Sciences, leading to the academic integration and centralized governance of these schools.

___E:Lee C. Bollinger U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Bollinger)___ became Columbia's 19th president in June 2002,  succeeding George Rupp.  He was appointed in October 2001 after arriving from the presidency of the University of Michigan.
His initiatives included the Manhattanville campus expansion into West Harlem, addressing space needs.
Bollinger launched the World Leaders Forum  and aimed to increase international student numbers.

He made a number of appointments to leadership roles including ___E:Jeffrey Sachs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_Sachs)___ ( ___E:Earth Institute U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Earth_Institute)___ ),  ___E:Alan Brinkley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Brinkley)___ (Provost),  ___E:Nicholas Lemann U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Lemann)___ (Journalism), David Hirsh (Research),  and ___E:Nicholas Dirks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Dirks)___ (Arts & Sciences).
Bollinger was the defendant in the Supreme Court's 2003 affirmative action cases ( Gratz and Grutter ), resulting in a split decision.
He consistently defended free speech principles during campus controversies involving faculty and students.

The university publicly launched a record $4 billion capital campaign in September 2006. Financial aid was improved, eliminating loans for undergraduates from families earning under $50,000, supported by a major gift from trustee ___E:Gerry Lenfest U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerry_Lenfest)___ .

Globalization efforts continued with the World Leaders Forum and the creation of the Committee on Global Thought, chaired by ___E:Joseph Stiglitz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Stiglitz)___ .

Columbia faculty received multiple Nobel Prizes: ___E:Richard Axel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Axel)___ and ___E:Linda Buck U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_B._Buck)___ (Medicine, 2004), ___E:Edmund Phelps U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_Phelps)___ (Economics, 2006), and ___E:Orhan Pamuk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk)___ (Literature, 2006). ___E:Václav Havel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%A1clav_Havel)___ joined the faculty.
Controversy erupted over a planned 2006 invitation to Iranian President Ahmadinejad, which was ultimately canceled due to logistical and security issues.
Later that year, a campus event featuring Minuteman Project speakers was disrupted by protesters.
Bollinger strongly condemned the disruption, reaffirming free speech principles while stating protesters do not have the right to silence speakers.
Several students faced disciplinary action, and non-affiliated individuals involved were banned from campus.

The ___E:2008 financial crisis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis)___ impacted Columbia's endowment, but less than peers as only 13% of the operating budget reliant on the endowment (compared to higher percentages at peers like ___E:Harvard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University)___ ).

The endowment recovered, hitting $8.2B in Oct 2013. Despite the downturn, Columbia pressed on with Manhattanville construction, receiving final state approval in June 2009. Major gifts fueled progress, including $400M from ___E:John Kluge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kluge)___ upon his death, $50M from the ___E:Vagelos U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vagelos_College_of_Physicians_and_Surgeons)___ family for the Medical Center, $100M from ___E:Henry Kravis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Kravis)___ for the Business School, $30M from Gerry Lenfest for an Arts center, and $200M from ___E:Mortimer Zuckerman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortimer_Zuckerman)___ for the Mind, Brain, Behavior Institute.

Following the repeal of "Don't Ask, Don't Tell," the University Senate voted 51–17 to invite ___E:ROTC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reserve_Officers%27_Training_Corps)___ back after a 40-year absence, and Bollinger announced an agreement with the Navy. Columbia expanded its ___E:Global Centers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Global_Centers)___ network (Amman, Beijing, Mumbai, Paris, Nairobi, Istanbul, Santiago), aiming to increase global engagement and international student enrollment (11% in CC in 2011, targeted higher).
From 2014 to 2021, Columbia University pursued significant physical expansion, notably opening major facilities on the Manhattanville campus (ZMBBI, Lenfest Center, The Forum).

Key strategic initiatives launched included the ___E:Knight First Amendment Institute U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knight_First_Amendment_Institute_v._Trump)___ , Columbia World Projects, and the new ___E:Columbia Climate School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Climate_School)___ (2020).

A $5 billion university capital campaign was launched (with a $1.5B A&S target), major gifts like $50M for A&S's Uris Hall renovation were secured, and the endowment grew significantly ($14.35B by mid-2021).

The COVID-19 pandemic starting March 2020 prompted remote operations, hiring/salary freezes, budget cuts, substantial borrowing (~$700M cited), and unpopular retirement contribution cuts, intensifying financial pressures.
Following accusations by ___E:Michael Thaddeus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Thaddeus)___ , a Columbia math professor, that Columbia submitted inaccurate data for college rankings, U.S.
News removed the university from its 2022 list, and Columbia later announced it would no longer participate.

Beginning in fall 2023, ___E:protests at Columbia University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_pro-Palestinian_campus_protests_and_occupations_during_the_Gaza_war)___ against the ___E:Gaza war U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war)___ and what the student protesters described as Columbia's complicity in the ___E:Gaza genocide U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_genocide)___ ,  including the ___E:Gaza Solidarity Encampment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_Solidarity_Encampment_(Columbia_University))___ (April 17–30, 2024), resulted in police action, student disciplinary measures, and the resignation of two university presidents: ___E:Minouche Shafik U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minouche_Shafik)___ and ___E:Katrina Armstrong U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katrina_Armstrong)___ .

The federal government then launched an ___E:investigation into antisemitism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisemitism_at_Columbia_University#During_the_Gaza_war)___ and withdrew funding, prompting the university to adopt stricter campus policies.

In July 2025, Columbia finalized a $220 million settlement to resume federal funding, agreeing to adopt the ___E:IHRA definition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IHRA_definition_of_antisemitism)___ of antisemitism, provide applicant data, and other policy changes while admitting no wrongdoing.

The majority of Columbia's graduate and undergraduate studies are conducted in the ___E:Upper Manhattan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Manhattan)___ neighborhood of ___E:Morningside Heights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morningside_Heights,_Manhattan)___ on ___E:Seth Low U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seth_Low)___ 's late-19th century vision of a university campus where all disciplines could be taught at one location.

The campus was designed along ___E:Beaux-Arts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaux-Arts_architecture)___ planning principles by the architects ___E:McKim, Mead & White U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McKim,_Mead_%26_White)___ .

Columbia's main campus occupies more than six ___E:city blocks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_block)___ , or 32 acres (13 ha), in Morningside Heights, New York City, a neighborhood that contains a number of academic institutions.
The university owns over 7,800 apartments in Morningside Heights, housing faculty, graduate students, and staff.
Almost two dozen undergraduate dormitories (purpose-built or converted) are located on campus or in Morningside Heights.

Columbia University has ___E:an extensive tunnel system U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_tunnels)___ , more than a century old, with the oldest portions predating the present campus.
Some of these remain accessible to the public, while others have been cordoned off.

___E:Butler Library U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butler_Library)___ is the largest in the ___E:Columbia University Libraries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_Libraries)___ system and one of the largest buildings on the campus.

It was completed in 1934 and renamed to Butler Library in 1946.  As of 2020 [update] , ___E:Columbia's library system U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_Library_System)___ includes over 15.0 million volumes, making it the eighth largest library system and fifth largest collegiate library system in the United States.
